r: The course's applied work is generating creative ideas and applying critical-thinking strategies to approach problems in novel ways, using the visual arts as an entry point. Task-exposure research places critical-thinking-intensive skills among the least exposed activities, which pushes the underlying competence down the exposure scale, even though the written idea-generation artifacts are more automatable. The binding near-term constraint is institutional: as a General Studies Arts and Humanities course it carries a GT-Pathways designation that mandates its transferable existence within the statutory general-education core. At 24 months the instrumental need is not eroded; a model can produce creative prose or brainstorm on demand, but the course exists to build the student's own habits of creative and critical thinking, dispelling the innate-talent myth it names. Rating Low, held by the transfer mandate rather than task characteristics alone.

By 2031, generative models will fluently brainstorm, reframe problems, and produce creative-thinking artifacts, weakening the rationale for students to generate them unaided. The instrumental case shifts toward the student's own cultivated ideation and toward judging which AI-surfaced ideas are actually novel or useful, a discernment the jagged-frontier evidence suggests grows more important as fluent output outruns reliability. The GT-Pathways Arts and Humanities mandate caps the erosion by holding the course in the general-education core across a catalog cycle, so despite writing's high task-exposure the rating settles at Medium rather than High. Creative and critical thinking as a durable human capacity is precisely the low-exposure category task-exposure research flags, but the course's applied outputs increasingly are not. The transfer lock and the reasoning core together keep it instrumentally necessary at this horizon.

A decade out, AI is a capable creative collaborator that generates and evaluates ideas on demand, and the rationale for producing the course's artifacts oneself is substantially eroded. Yet the general-education Arts and Humanities requirement persists in the central case, and a cultivated capacity to think creatively and critically, to recognize when a fluent AI suggestion is shallow or wrong, retains value the tool does not supply to the learner. The rating holds Medium, capped by the transfer mandate from rising to High and lifted above Low by that same lock. The genuine uncertainty is pedagogical: how a creativity course is taught and assessed when ideation is ubiquitous, not whether the general-education requirement and its thinking-skills aim remain in force, which in the central case they do. Confidence is moderate given the course's broad, skills-oriented description.
ARTE 2060.d: This course introduces contemporary ideas and strategies exploring creative thinking informed by the visual arts. Students are exposed to the interconnectedness of creative and critical thinking and develop strategies for thinking that embrace the habits of creativity, dispelling the myth that people are born creative or uncreative. Using the visual arts as an entry point for the development of creative and critical-thinking skills, students learn how to approach problems in novel ways.

Rating Low, anchored by embodiment.

By 2031, generative image models will be ubiquitous and will reshape commercial image production, and AI will more readily draft the documentary and analytical writing the course requires. That is largely an economic and artifact-level shift; whether an arts-based-research student still needs embodied studio practice and firsthand field observation is unchanged, because the psychomotor act of art-making and the situated reading of real creative environments resist substitution. A plausible migration is that some documentation synthesis moves to AI, echoing writing's high task-exposure, but the studio and field core does not. Absent any institutional mandate, embodiment alone holds the instrumental case at Low across this horizon. The discipline's market for images is exposed; the course's field-and-studio task necessity is not, and no model conducts the fieldwork on the student's behalf.

Over a decade, AI image generation will be woven through visual culture and will handle much analytical writing, and the wide-uncertainty caveat is real for the visual-arts labor market. But Tracing Thought builds an embodied human competence, physical studio technique plus firsthand observation of creative practice in diverse settings, that is not a task AI performs for the student; base automatability ticks up only as the documentation and semiotic-analysis layer encroaches, while embodiment keeps the rating Low even at 2036. The honest framing is that the instrumental case rests on the human acts of making art and observing people making it, which endure even as the market for images and the tooling for analysis transform around them. Rating holds Low, carried by embodiment rather than any external mandate.
ARTE 3333.d: This studio-based course uses Arts Based Research which uses the arts as objects of inquiry as well as modes of investigation. It integrates field research with creative practice to investigate how art-making environments develop create thought. Students will conduct research field hours in culturally and linguistically diverse art-making spaces, observing how people engage in the creative processes and how their thinking is expressed through poetic, visual form. In the studio, students will translate these encounters into original artworks that critically reflect on the semiotics of representation-the ways signs, images, and symbols convey meaning in creative practice. An additional component of the course is producing a Reggio Emilia-inspired documentation board that synthesize field observations, visual analysis, and reflective writing into layered narratives of creative thinking. By combining research, artmaking, and interpretive documentation, students will expand their ability to analyze, synthesize, and represent human creativity while developing their own artistic voice.

By 2031, AI will fluently deliver and synthesize the history and philosophy of art education and help draft teaching-philosophy statements, substantially automating the knowledge-transmission the course provides. Yet the approved-program licensure mandate continues to require this foundational component within the art-education curriculum, and the licensure clock does not turn within a catalog cycle or two, so the institutional cap holds the rating at Low even as the applied tasks become AI-deliverable. Evaluating competing philosophical and legal claims about art education, and detecting where fluent AI synthesis is confidently wrong, retains a verification role for the trained candidate. This is a case where capability outruns institutional change; the rating tracks the binding mandate rather than the exposure of the writing tasks, which on their own would read distinctly higher.

A decade out, AI generates scholarship-grade synthesis of art-education history and philosophy on demand, and the execution rationale for the course's knowledge tasks is largely eroded. The rating rises to Medium, since the applied synthesis tasks are highly automatable and the mandate is no longer certain to hold the course in its current form, though the field-observation component and the possibility of a continued mandate keep it from High. The Low-Low-Medium trajectory reflects capability held back by a licensure clock that only loosens at the long horizon; confidence is moderate on the timing of any accreditor change.
ARTE 3601.d: Students in this course explore the historical, philosophical, social, political, legal, psychological, and educational factors that have influenced-and continue to influence-how art education is taught in the United States. Learning is enriched through 20 hours of field observation, where theory from lectures and readings connects directly to classroom practice. Throughout the course, students are encouraged to cultivate a personal teaching philosophy for art that will guide their instructional practices and foster their development as reflective educators.

r: The applied work is designing and implementing curriculum for inclusive, mainstreamed art classrooms and, through 10 hours of field observation, working directly with pre-K-12 students across a range of exceptionalities on engagement, individualization, and classroom management. Curriculum drafting is partially exposed to AI, but the graded core is in-person, real-time interpersonal judgment with vulnerable minors, squarely in the low-exposure, high-presence categories task-exposure research flags as resistant, with a verification burden heightened by special-education stakes. At 24 months the instrumental need to develop embodied inclusive-classroom competence is untouched; a model can suggest accommodations, but it does not manage or individualize instruction for real children in the room. Rating Low.

By 2031, AI will increasingly assist with differentiated lesson design, accommodation generation, and progress analytics, and those tools will appear in inclusive art classrooms. That augments the teacher; it does not perform the embodied work of engaging, individualizing for, and managing a diverse group of exceptional learners in person, which is what the field component develops. Child-welfare and special-education stakes keep the verification burden real and a knowledgeable human in the loop, and the Colorado licensure field-hour mandate does not relax within a catalog cycle. Embodiment and institutional lock-in together preserve the instrumental case; AI changes what candidates learn to oversee, the automated accommodation or the generated plan, not whether they must be in the classroom practicing inclusive instruction. Even with a decade of capability growth and broad classroom AI adoption, the requirement that art-education candidates accumulate supervised, in-person field hours working directly with exceptional pre-K-12 students is among the more durable constraints in the catalog, with no central-case path to removal by 2036. The embodied, interpersonal nature of inclusive instruction resists direct substitution, and the special-education context sustains a real verification premium on the human who understands what an AI recommendation would get wrong for a specific child. The genuine uncertainty is how heavily AI mediates curriculum and assessment, not whether the field requirement and the human competence it certifies remain necessary. Rating holds Low; here embodiment and the licensure mandate reinforce each other rather than either acting alone.
ARTE 3605.d: Students in this lecture/field experience course address the necessary steps needed to create and implement effective curriculum in an inclusive or mainstreamed art classroom. Students learn about various exceptionalities of pre k-12 students, ranging from mild to severe. The challenge to meet the individualized needs of a diverse student population through effective instruction is explored in the classroom and in the field. During the semester students complete 10 hours of field observations working directly with students, putting into practice the theories discussed in-class. Pre-service art education students develop effective techniques for fostering student engagement, individualization strategies, problem solving, and classroom management techniques while working in an inclusive learning environment.

ARTE 4130.d: Students in this lecture/studio course develop age- appropriate curriculum and instructional methodologies for teaching that will foster fluency, flexibility and ingenuity in the elementary art classroom. Students draw connections between concepts developed in class, studio practices, and discussions based on observations made in the concurrent field experience, ARTE 4140 - Field Experience: Art Education Elementary. Using these skills, students explore, analyze, and formulate pedagogical strategies necessary to become informed practitioners and advocates within the field of art education.

r: The applied activity is a fifty-hour immersive field experience working directly with a mentor teacher in an elementary classroom, applying classroom management, budgeting, and community-engagement practices while fostering children's intellectual and artistic growth, in accordance with Colorado Teacher Quality Standards. ARTE 4140.d: Students take this field experience course concurrently with ARTE 4130 - Elementary Art Education: Curriculum and Instruction. During the fifty-hour field experience, preservice art education students work directly with a mentor teacher in the classroom fostering an understanding of the intellectual and artistic growth of elementary school children. In an immersive field experience, application of practical issues such as classroom management, budgeting, and community engagement are experienced by the student, building an informed understanding of pedagogical practices needed for a professional career at the elementary school level. Successful completion of the field experience is in accordance with Teacher Quality Standards and Colorado Academic Standards: Visual Arts.

ARTE 4230.d: Students in this course develop age-appropriate curriculum and instructional methodologies for teaching art that foster fluency, flexibility and ingenuity for grades 6-12. ARTE 4701.d: Students in this course complete supervised, full-time, sixteen-week, student teaching experience in an accredited public or private elementary and secondary school. During the student teaching experience students take responsibility for the instruction, assessment, and supervision of an identified group of learners at K-12 grade levels. Regularly scheduled observations at both eight-week placements, and ten hours of seminar conducted by an appointed university supervisor are part of the student teaching requirement. Teacher candidates must complete a Teacher Work Sample and be rated as proficient in all Teacher Quality Standards for Colorado teachers to receive MSU Denver's recommendation for licensure.

ARTE 4715.d: This elective course addresses the needs of individual, advanced, senior-level students completing the Art Education concentration who want to pursue a focused study of a pedagogical problem. Students reflect upon their prior learning in art education and their studio art concentrations, identifying the interdisciplinary learning connections that they have made through courses that have influenced their professional knowledge in the field of teaching. Evidence of these influential learning connections is documented and presented in a professional portfolio. Students plan, instruct and assess a one-week studio workshop for students in grades K-12.

ARTE 4850.d: This course is an interdisciplinary studio art class that addresses the need for art education students and K-12 Art Licensure candidates to link their professional practice as artists with their practice as educators. Students will create a portfolio of work that is conceptually driven, and seek out a variety of materials that will best express their vision. Students will be responsible for scheduling, preparing and presenting their portfolio of work in a professional format as a visiting artist in a K-12 art classroom.
